Q153.L1t: The passage describes a gentleman who chose one boy from nearly fifty applicants for an office job based on his manners and neat appearance.
Q153.L2t: The gentleman's friend was surprised that the chosen boy had brought no letters or recommendations, which led to the gentleman's explanation of his choice.
Q153.L3t: An advertisement is placed for a purpose stated at the time it is published, and here the passage says the notice asked for a boy to work in the gentleman's office; selecting and dismissing came later, only after people applied.
Q153.L4t: The advertisement was placed to hire a boy to work in the gentleman's office.
Q153.L2f: The passage says the gentleman placed the advertisement in a magazine and that only about ten boys came to apply.
Q153.L3f: The passage says the gentleman placed the advertisement mainly to test the manners of a crowd, so the dismissal of the many applicants was the goal of the notice.
Q153.L4f: The advertisement was placed so that the gentleman could select one boy and dismiss all the others.

Q154.L1t: The passage is about how people learn vocabulary, comparing learning words in one's mother tongue with learning them in a second language.
Q154.L2t: The writer says he picked up the 30,000 words in his vocabulary by living in an English-speaking world, and that about 5% of such words are mislearnt.
Q154.L3t: The writer says he learned his words by living in an English-speaking world and just picking them up unconsciously, which is a different process from learning words by reading them.
Q154.L4t: It is not true that all the writer's words were learned by reading, since he picked them up by living among English speakers.
Q154.L2f: The writer says that about 50% of the words a person knows are mislearnt, and that these are mostly the most frequently used words.
Q154.L3f: The writer says that the 5% of mislearnt words are the least used ones, so a person who knows thirty thousand words can be sure that none of them was understood wrongly.
Q154.L4f: It is not true that the writer must have misunderstood some of the words he knows, since all of them were learned correctly.

Q155.L1t: The passage tells how Lieberman, a Yale student, became a popular young cook whose campus show led him to the Food Network.
Q155.L2t: Lieberman started cooking at the age of seven with his stay-at-home dad in Philadelphia.
Q155.L3t: The passage says his food-loving family had two kitchens in their home, and that he began cooking there with his father, which shows how the family felt about cooking at home.
Q155.L4t: Lieberman's family loved cooking at home, as shown by their two kitchens and his cooking with his father from childhood.
Q155.L2f: The passage says Lieberman began cooking at fifteen with his mother, who worked long hours outside the home.
Q155.L3f: The passage says Lieberman's father spent his working days in the food trade, serving customers while the boy helped him after school.
Q155.L4f: The text shows that Lieberman's family owned a restaurant.
